claim: Notch-RBP-J signaling plays an essential role in the maintenance of myeloid homeostasis.
source: Notch-RBP-J signaling plays an essential role in the maintenance of myeloid homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data in this manuscript.

claim: The role of Notch-RBP-J signaling pathway in monocyte cell fate decisions is not fully understood.
source: However, its role in monocyte cell fate decisions is not fully understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Conditional deletion of transcription factor RBP-J in myeloid cells resulted in marked accumulation of blood Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: Here, we showed that conditional deletion of transcription factor RBP-J in myeloid cells resulted in marked accumulation of blood Ly6Clo monocytes that highly expressed chemokine receptor CCR2.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RBP-J-deficient blood Ly6Clo monocytes highly expressed chemokine receptor CCR2.
source: Here, we showed that conditional deletion of transcription factor RBP-J in myeloid cells resulted in marked accumulation of blood Ly6Clo monocytes that highly expressed chemokine receptor CCR2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There is a cell-intrinsic requirement of RBP-J for controlling blood Ly6CloCCR2hi monocytes.
source: Bone marrow transplantation and parabiosis experiments revealed a cell-intrinsic requirement of RBP-J for controlling blood Ly6CloCCR2hi monocytes.
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow transplantation data in Figure 3B and parabiosis data in Figure 3E.

claim: RBP-J-deficient Ly6Clo monocytes exhibited enhanced capacity competing with wildtype counterparts in blood circulation.
source: RBP-J-deficient Ly6Clo monocytes exhibited enhanced capacity competing with wildtype counterparts in blood circulation.
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: RBP-J deficiency led to markedly increased population of lung tissues with Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: In accordance with alterations of circulating monocytes, RBP-J deficiency led to markedly increased population of lung tissues with Ly6Clo monocytes and CD16.2+ interstitial macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: RBP-J deficiency led to markedly increased population of lung tissues with CD16.2+ interstitial macrophages.
source: In accordance with alterations of circulating monocytes, RBP-J deficiency led to markedly increased population of lung tissues with Ly6Clo monocytes and CD16.2+ interstitial macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: RBP-J deficiency-associated phenotypes could be genetically corrected by further deleting Ccr2 in myeloid cells.
source: Furthermore, RBP-J deficiency-associated phenotypes could be genetically corrected by further deleting Ccr2 in myeloid cells.
evidence: This is supported by data from double knockout mice shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: RBP-J functions as a crucial regulator of blood Ly6Clo monocytes at least in part through regulation of CCR2.
source: These results demonstrate that RBP-J functions as a crucial regulator of blood Ly6Clo monocytes and thus derived lung-resident myeloid populations, at least in part through regulation of CCR2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic rescue experiments with CCR2 deletion shown in Figure 5.

claim: Monocytes are integral components of the mononuclear phagocyte system that develop from monocyte precursors in the bone marrow.
source: Monocytes are integral components of the mononuclear phagocyte system that develop from monocyte precursors in the bone marrow (Guilliams et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Several functionally and phenotypically distinct subsets of blood monocytes have been defined on the basis of expression of surface markers.
source: Several functionally and phenotypically distinct subsets of blood monocytes have been defined on the basis of expression of surface markers (Cros et al., 2010; Geissmann et al., 2003; Passlick et al., 1989; Weber et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In mice, Ly6Chi monocytes are characterized by Ly6ChiCCR2hiCX3CR1lo.
source: In mice, Ly6Chi monocytes (also called inflammatory or classical monocytes) characterized by Ly6ChiCCR2hiCX3CR1lo exhibit a short half-life and are recruited to tissue and differentiate into macrophages and dendritic cells (Ginhoux and Jung, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ly6Chi monocytes exhibit a short half-life.
source: In mice, Ly6Chi monocytes (also called inflammatory or classical monocytes) characterized by Ly6ChiCCR2hiCX3CR1lo exhibit a short half-life and are recruited to tissue and differentiate into macrophages and dendritic cells (Ginhoux and Jung, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ly6Chi monocytes are recruited to tissue and differentiate into macrophages and dendritic cells.
source: In mice, Ly6Chi monocytes (also called inflammatory or classical monocytes) characterized by Ly6ChiCCR2hiCX3CR1lo exhibit a short half-life and are recruited to tissue and differentiate into macrophages and dendritic cells (Ginhoux and Jung, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ly6Chi monocytes are analogous to CD14+ human monocytes based on gene expression profiling.
source: Ly6Chi monocytes are analogous to CD14+ human monocytes based on gene expression profiling (Ingersoll et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes express high level of CX3CR1 and low level of CCR2.
source: A second subtype of monocytes is called Ly6Clo monocytes (also termed patrolling monocytes or non-classical monocytes), which express high level of CX3CR1 and low level of CCR2, equivalent to CD14loCD16+ human monocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about monocyte phenotypes.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes are equivalent to CD14loCD16+ human monocytes.
source: A second subtype of monocytes is called Ly6Clo monocytes (also termed patrolling monocytes or non-classical monocytes), which express high level of CX3CR1 and low level of CCR2, equivalent to CD14loCD16+ human monocytes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about monocyte phenotypes.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes are regarded as blood-resident macrophages that patrol blood vessels and scavenge microparticles attached to the endothelium under physiological conditions.
source: Ly6Clo monocytes are regarded as blood-resident macrophages that patrol blood vessels and scavenge microparticles attached to the endothelium under physiological conditions, and exhibit a long half-life in the steady state (Auffray et al., 2007; Carlin et al., 2013; Yona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes exhibit a long half-life in the steady state.
source: Ly6Clo monocytes are regarded as blood-resident macrophages that patrol blood vessels and scavenge microparticles attached to the endothelium under physiological conditions, and exhibit a long half-life in the steady state (Auffray et al., 2007; Carlin et al., 2013; Yona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes may exert a protective effect by suppressing atherosclerosis in mice.
source: Ly6Clo monocytes may exert a protective effect by suppressing atherosclerosis in mice, while high levels of non-classical monocytes have been associated with more advanced vascular dysfunction and oxidative stress in patients with coronary artery disease (Hamers et al., 2012; Hanna et al., 2012; Urbanski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: High levels of non-classical monocytes have been associated with more advanced vascular dysfunction and oxidative stress in patients with coronary artery disease.
source: Ly6Clo monocytes may exert a protective effect by suppressing atherosclerosis in mice, while high levels of non-classical monocytes have been associated with more advanced vascular dysfunction and oxidative stress in patients with coronary artery disease (Hamers et al., 2012; Hanna et al., 2012; Urbanski et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In inflammatory settings, Ly6Clo monocytes often show anti-inflammatory properties.
source: In the inflammatory settings, Ly6Clo monocytes often show anti-inflammatory properties, yet also exhibit a proinflammatory role under certain circumstances (Amano et al., 2005; Brunet et al., 2016; Carlin et al., 2013; Cros et al., 2010; Misharin et al., 2014; Nahrendorf et al., 2007; Puchner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes exhibit a proinflammatory role under certain circumstances.
source: In the inflammatory settings, Ly6Clo monocytes often show anti-inflammatory properties, yet also exhibit a proinflammatory role under certain circumstances (Amano et al., 2005; Brunet et al., 2016; Carlin et al., 2013; Cros et al., 2010; Misharin et al., 2014; Nahrendorf et al., 2007; Puchner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes have demonstrated protective functions in tumorigenesis, such as engulfing tumor materials to prevent cancer metastasis.
source: In addition, Ly6Clo monocytes have demonstrated protective functions in tumorigenesis, such as engulfing tumor materials to prevent cancer metastasis, activating and recruiting NK cells to the lungs (Hanna et al., 2015; Thomas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes activate and recruit NK cells to the lungs.
source: In addition, Ly6Clo monocytes have demonstrated protective functions in tumorigenesis, such as engulfing tumor materials to prevent cancer metastasis, activating and recruiting NK cells to the lungs (Hanna et al., 2015; Thomas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The generation and maintenance of Ly6Clo monocytes are regulated by several transcription factors, including Nr4a1 and CEBPβ.
source: The generation and maintenance of Ly6Clo monocytes are regulated by several transcription factors, including Nr4a1 and CEBPβ (Hanna et al., 2011; Tamura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) signaling pathway is important for the generation and survival of Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: The colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) signaling pathway is important for the generation and survival of Ly6Clo monocytes, and neutralizing antibodies against CSF1R can reduce their numbers (MacDonald et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Neutralizing antibodies against CSF1R can reduce the numbers of Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: The colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) signaling pathway is important for the generation and survival of Ly6Clo monocytes, and neutralizing antibodies against CSF1R can reduce their numbers (MacDonald et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Different subsets of monocytes may be supported by distinct cellular sources of CSF-1 within bone marrow niches.
source: Interestingly, recent studies have suggested that different subsets of monocytes may be supported by distinct cellular sources of CSF-1 within bone marrow niches, in which targeted deletion of Csf1 from sinusoidal endothelial cells selectively reduces Ly6Clo monocytes but not Ly6Chi monocytes (Emoto et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Targeted deletion of Csf1 from sinusoidal endothelial cells selectively reduces Ly6Clo monocytes but not Ly6Chi monocytes.
source: Interestingly, recent studies have suggested that different subsets of monocytes may be supported by distinct cellular sources of CSF-1 within bone marrow niches, in which targeted deletion of Csf1 from sinusoidal endothelial cells selectively reduces Ly6Clo monocytes but not Ly6Chi monocytes (Emoto et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: LAIR1 is activated by stromal protein Colec12.
source: LAIR1 has been shown to be activated by stromal protein Colec12, and LAIR1 deficiency leads to aberrant proliferation and apoptosis in bone marrow non-classical monocytes (Keerthivasan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: LAIR1 deficiency leads to aberrant proliferation and apoptosis in bone marrow non-classical monocytes.
source: LAIR1 has been shown to be activated by stromal protein Colec12, and LAIR1 deficiency leads to aberrant proliferation and apoptosis in bone marrow non-classical monocytes (Keerthivasan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: RBP-J is commonly known as the master nuclear mediator of canonical Notch signaling.
source: Recombinant recognition sequence binding protein at the Jκ site (RBP-J; also named CSL) is commonly known as the master nuclear mediator of canonical Notch signaling (Radtke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In the absence of Notch intracellular domain, RBP-J associates with co-repressor proteins to repress transcription of downstream target genes.
source: In the absence of Notch intracellular domain, RBP-J associates with co-repressor proteins to repress transcription of downstream target genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RBP-J function.

claim: The best studied functions of Notch signaling are its roles in regulating the development of lymphocytes, such as T cells and marginal zone B cells.
source: In the immune system, the best studied functions of Notch signaling are its roles in regulating the development of lymphocytes, such as T cells and marginal zone B cells (Radtke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Notch signaling has been reported to regulate the differentiation and function of myeloid cells including granulocyte/monocyte progenitors, osteoclasts, and dendritic cells.
source: Notch signaling also has been reported to regulate the differentiation and function of myeloid cells including granulocyte/monocyte progenitors, osteoclasts, and dendritic cells (Caton et al., 2007; Klinakis et al., 2011; Lewis et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In osteoclasts, RBP-J represses osteoclastogenesis, particularly under inflammatory conditions.
source: In osteoclasts, RBP-J represses osteoclastogenesis, particularly under inflammatory conditions (Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In dendritic cells, Notch-RBP-J signaling controls the maintenance of CD8- DC.
source: In dendritic cells, Notch-RBP-J signaling controls the maintenance of CD8- DC (Caton et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Notch2-RBP-J pathway is essential for the development of CD8-ESAM+ DC in the spleen.
source: In addition, Notch2-RBP-J pathway is essential for the development of CD8-ESAM+ DC in the spleen and CD103+CD11b+ DC in the lamina propria of the intestine (Lewis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Notch2-RBP-J pathway is essential for the development of CD103+CD11b+ DC in the lamina propria of the intestine.
source: In addition, Notch2-RBP-J pathway is essential for the development of CD8-ESAM+ DC in the spleen and CD103+CD11b+ DC in the lamina propria of the intestine (Lewis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: RBP-J controlled homeostasis of blood Ly6Clo monocytes in a cell-intrinsic manner.
source: Here, we demonstrated that RBP-J controlled homeostasis of blood Ly6Clo monocytes in a cell-intrinsic manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by bone marrow transplantation and parabiosis experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: RBP-J deficiency led to a drastic increase in blood Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: RBP-J deficiency led to a drastic increase in blood Ly6Clo monocytes, lung Ly6Clo monocytes, and CD16.2+ IM.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1A.

claim: RBP-J deficiency led to a drastic increase in lung Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: RBP-J deficiency led to a drastic increase in blood Ly6Clo monocytes, lung Ly6Clo monocytes, and CD16.2+ IM.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: RBP-J deficiency led to a drastic increase in CD16.2+ IM.
source: RBP-J deficiency led to a drastic increase in blood Ly6Clo monocytes, lung Ly6Clo monocytes, and CD16.2+ IM.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: RBP-J plays a critical role in regulating the population and characteristics of Ly6Clo monocytes in the blood and lung.
source: Our results suggest that RBP-J plays a critical role in regulating the population and characteristics of Ly6Clo monocytes in the blood and lung.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Efficient deletion of Rbpj in blood monocytes was confirmed by quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR).
source: Efficient deletion of Rbpj in blood monocytes was confirmed by quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RBP-J-deficient mice had a significant increase in the proportion of Ly6Clo monocytes in blood, compared to age-matched control mice.
source: Flow cytometric analysis revealed that RBP-J-deficient mice had a significant increase in the proportion of Ly6Clo monocytes, but not Ly6Chi monocytes, in blood, compared to age-matched control mice with the genotype Rbpj+/+Lyz2cre/cre (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RBP-J-deficient mice did not have a significant increase in the proportion of Ly6Chi monocytes in blood.
source: Flow cytometric analysis revealed that RBP-J-deficient mice had a significant increase in the proportion of Ly6Clo monocytes, but not Ly6Chi monocytes, in blood, compared to age-matched control mice with the genotype Rbpj+/+Lyz2cre/cre (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: RBP-J-deficient mice exhibited minimal alterations in the percentages of monocyte subsets in bone marrow.
source: In contrast to circulating monocytes, RBP-J-deficient mice exhibited minimal alterations in the percentages of monocyte subsets in bone marrow (BM) and spleen (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RBP-J-deficient mice exhibited minimal alterations in the percentages of monocyte subsets in spleen.
source: In contrast to circulating monocytes, RBP-J-deficient mice exhibited minimal alterations in the percentages of monocyte subsets in bone marrow (BM) and spleen (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RBP-J deficiency in myeloid cells did not appear to have an effect on neutrophils.
source: Additionally, RBP-J deficiency in myeloid cells did not appear to have an effect on neutrophils (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Among circulating myeloid populations, RBP-J selectively controlled the subset of Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: Therefore, among circulating myeloid populations, RBP-J selectively controlled the subset of Ly6Clo monocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that only Ly6Clo monocytes were affected in blood.

claim: BM progenitors that give rise to circulating monocytes are monocyte-dendritic cell progenitors (MDPs) and common monocyte progenitors (cMoPs).
source: BM progenitors that give rise to circulating monocytes are monocyte-dendritic cell progenitors (MDPs) and common monocyte progenitors (cMoPs) (Hanna et al., 2011; Hettinger et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2019; Varol et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The percentages of MDPs and cMoPs were equivalent in control and RBP-J-deficient mice.
source: Next, we analyzed BM progenitors and found that the percentages of MDPs and cMoPs were equivalent in control and RBP-J-deficient mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Alterations of peripheral blood Ly6Clo monocytes may not originate from BM.
source: These results in conjunction with the observations of normal BM monocyte populations, suggest that alterations of peripheral blood Ly6Clo monocytes may not originate from BM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that BM monocyte populations and progenitors are normal.

claim: RBP-J deficiency did not affect egress of Ly6Clo monocytes from BM.
source: The results showed that RBP-J deficiency did not affect egress of Ly6Clo monocytes from BM (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo labeling data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: RBP-J is a critical regulator controlling homeostasis of peripheral blood Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: Taken together, these data revealed RBP-J as a critical regulator controlling homeostasis of peripheral blood Ly6Clo monocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: The increase in blood Ly6Clo monocytes in RBP-J-deficient mice was not due to decreased cell death.
source: We first stained monocytes with Annexin V and 7-amino-actinomycin D (7-AAD) to identify apoptotic cells and observed comparable percentages of apoptotic blood Ly6Clo monocytes in control and RBP-J-deficient mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Annexin V staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nr4a1 plays a crucial role in the survival of Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: Given the crucial role of Nr4a1 in the survival of Ly6Clo monocytes (Hanna et al., 2011), we detected the expression of Nr4a1, which was similar in Ly6Clo monocytes from control and RBP-J-deficient mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The expression of Nr4a1 was similar in Ly6Clo monocytes from control and RBP-J-deficient mice.
source: Given the crucial role of Nr4a1 in the survival of Ly6Clo monocytes (Hanna et al., 2011), we detected the expression of Nr4a1, which was similar in Ly6Clo monocytes from control and RBP-J-deficient mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ki-67 levels in blood monocytes displayed no differences between control and RBP-J-deficient mice.
source: Ki-67 levels in blood monocytes displayed no differences between control and RBP-J-deficient mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The percentage of EdU+ monocytes did not significantly differ between control and RBP-J-deficient mice at the indicated time points.
source: The percentage of EdU+ monocytes did not significantly differ between control and RBP-J-deficient mice at the indicated time points, implying that the turnover of Ly6Clo monocytes was normal in RBP-J-deficient mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The turnover of Ly6Clo monocytes was normal in RBP-J-deficient mice.
source: The percentage of EdU+ monocytes did not significantly differ between control and RBP-J-deficient mice at the indicated time points, implying that the turnover of Ly6Clo monocytes was normal in RBP-J-deficient mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Fluorescent latex beads as particulate tracers could be phagocytosed by monocytes after intravenous injection and stably label Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: Fluorescent latex beads as particulate tracers could be phagocytosed by monocytes after intravenous injection and stably label Ly6Clo monocytes (Tacke et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: By day 7 post injection, only Ly6Clo monocytes were latex+ as previously reported.
source: By day 7 post injection, only Ly6Clo monocytes were latex+ as previously reported (Tacke et al., 2006), whereas control and RBP-J-deficient mice groups presented a similar frequency of latex+ monocytes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Control and RBP-J-deficient mice groups presented a similar frequency of latex+ monocytes.
source: By day 7 post injection, only Ly6Clo monocytes were latex+ as previously reported (Tacke et al., 2006), whereas control and RBP-J-deficient mice groups presented a similar frequency of latex+ monocytes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by latex beads labeling data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: RBP-J did not influence monocyte survival and proliferation.
source: Together, these data indicated that RBP-J did not influence monocyte survival and proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the apoptosis, Ki-67, EdU, and latex beads data.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes are observed in recipient mice following the adoptive transfer of Ly6Chi monocytes.
source: Previous studies have shown that Ly6Clo monocytes are observed in recipient mice following the adoptive transfer of Ly6Chi monocytes, indicating that Ly6Chi monocytes can convert into Ly6Clo monocytes (Varol et al., 2007; Yona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ly6Chi monocytes can convert into Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: Previous studies have shown that Ly6Clo monocytes are observed in recipient mice following the adoptive transfer of Ly6Chi monocytes, indicating that Ly6Chi monocytes can convert into Ly6Clo monocytes (Varol et al., 2007; Yona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sixty hours after transfer, a subset of cells from donors were converted into Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: Sixty hours after transfer, a subset of cells from donors were converted into Ly6Clo monocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and equal percentages of Ly6Clo monocytes were derived from control and Rbpjfl/flLyz2cre/creCx3cr1gfp/+ donors (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Equal percentages of Ly6Clo monocytes were derived from control and Rbpjfl/flLyz2cre/creCx3cr1gfp/+ donors.
source: Sixty hours after transfer, a subset of cells from donors were converted into Ly6Clo monocytes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and equal percentages of Ly6Clo monocytes were derived from control and Rbpjfl/flLyz2cre/creCx3cr1gfp/+ donors (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The conversion of Ly6Chi monocyte into Ly6Clo monocyte was not affected by RBP-J deficiency.
source: Thus, the conversion of Ly6Chi monocyte into Ly6Clo monocyte was not affected by RBP-J deficiency.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the adoptive transfer data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The increase in Ly6Clo monocytes in RBP-J-deficient mice was BM-derived.
source: We next wondered whether the increase in Ly6Clo monocytes in RBP-J-deficient mice was BM-derived and cell-intrinsic.
evidence: This is a question that was addressed by bone marrow transplantation experiments.

claim: The frequencies of CD45.2+ cells within total cells were similar to the mixture ratio of BM cells for Ly6Chi monocytes and neutrophils in both BM and blood.
source: Eight weeks after transplantation, we analyzed the frequencies of CD45.2+ donor cells in the BM and blood of recipient mice and found that the frequencies of CD45.2+ cells within total cells were similar to the mixture ratio of BM cells for Ly6Chi monocytes and neutrophils in both BM and blood (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow transplantation data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: More blood Ly6Clo monocytes were derived from RBP-J-deficient donors than control donors.
source: Specifically, more blood Ly6Clo monocytes were derived from RBP-J-deficient donors than control donors (Figure 3B), reflecting that the contribution of RBP-J-deficient cells in blood Ly6Clo cells was significantly higher than that of control cells.
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow transplantation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The contribution of RBP-J-deficient cells in blood Ly6Clo cells was significantly higher than that of control cells.
source: Specifically, more blood Ly6Clo monocytes were derived from RBP-J-deficient donors than control donors (Figure 3B), reflecting that the contribution of RBP-J-deficient cells in blood Ly6Clo cells was significantly higher than that of control cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on bone marrow transplantation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RBP-J-deficient BM cells were highly efficient in generating blood Ly6Clo monocytes.
source: These results implied that RBP-J-deficient BM cells were highly efficient in generating blood Ly6Clo monocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on bone marrow transplantation data.

claim: About 50% of B cells and T cells in parabiotic mice displayed efficient exchange of their circulation.
source: Four weeks after the procedure, about 50% of B cells and T cells in parabiotic mice displayed efficient exchange of their circulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RBP-J-deficient mice exhibited higher percentages of Ly6Clo monocytes than control animals in parabiosis experiments.
source: As expected, RBP-J-deficient mice exhibited higher percentages of Ly6Clo monocytes than control animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the parabiotic Cx3cr1gfp/+ mice, RBP-J-deficient cells still constituted significantly higher proportion of circulating Ly6Clo monocytes than RBP-J sufficient counterparts.
source: Intriguingly, in the parabiotic Cx3cr1gfp/+ mice, RBP-J-deficient cells still constituted significantly higher proportion of circulating Ly6Clo, but not Ly6Chi monocytes, than RBP-J sufficient counterparts as indicated by the percentages of the GFP-negative population (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In the parabiotic Cx3cr1gfp/+ mice, RBP-J-deficient cells did not constitute significantly higher proportion of circulating Ly6Chi monocytes than RBP-J sufficient counterparts.
source: Intriguingly, in the parabiotic Cx3cr1gfp/+ mice, RBP-J-deficient cells still constituted significantly higher proportion of circulating Ly6Clo, but not Ly6Chi monocytes, than RBP-J sufficient counterparts as indicated by the percentages of the GFP-negative population (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by parabiosis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The enhanced ability of Ly6Clo monocytes to circulate in the peripheral blood as a result of RBP-J deficiency was cell-intrinsic.
source: These results implicated that the enhanced ability of Ly6Clo monocytes to circulate in the peripheral blood as a result of RBP-J deficiency was cell-intrinsic.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on parabiosis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes in RBP-J-deficient mice exhibited low expression of Itgax but high expression of Ccr2, in comparison to those in control mice.
source: To further study the consequences of RBP-J loss of function in blood Ly6Clo monocytes, we performed gene expression profiling by RNA-seq, which revealed that Ly6Clo monocytes in RBP-J-deficient mice exhibited low expression of Itgax but high expression of Ccr2, in comparison to those in control mice (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Differential expression patterns of phenotypic marker genes were confirmed by qPCR and flow cytometry analysis.
source: These differential expression patterns of phenotypic marker genes were also confirmed by qPCR and flow cytometry analysis (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Blood Ly6Chi monocytes and BM monocytes displayed normal levels of CD11c and CCR2.
source: However, blood Ly6Chi monocytes and BM monocytes displayed normal levels of CD11c and CCR2 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Principal component analysis showed distinct expression pattern of monocytes between control and RBP-J-deficient mice.
source: Moreover, principal component analysis showed distinct expression pattern of monocytes between control and RBP-J-deficient mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ly6Clo monocytes derived from RBP-J-deficient BM cells expressed high levels of CCR2 but low levels of CD11c, in comparison to those derived from control BM cells.
source: The findings indicated that Ly6Clo monocytes derived from RBP-J-deficient BM cells expressed high levels of CCR2 but low levels of CD11c, in comparison to those derived from control BM cells, whereas no significant changes were observed in blood Ly6Chi and BM monocytes, as expected (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by bone marrow transplantation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No significant changes in CCR2 and CD11c expression were observed in blood Ly6Chi and BM monocytes derived from RBP-J-deficient BM cells.
